<p><i><b>Adventure Time</b></i><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-note12_10-0"><a href="#cite_note-note12-10"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>c<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is an American <a href="/wiki/Fantasy" title="Fantasy">fantasy</a> <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Animated_television_series" title="Animated television series">animated television series</a> created by <a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Ward" title="Pendleton Ward">Pendleton Ward</a> and co-produced by <a href="/wiki/Frederator_Studios" title="Frederator Studios">Frederator Studios</a> for <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a>. The series follows the adventures of a boy named <a href="/wiki/Finn_the_Human" title="Finn the Human">Finn</a> (<a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Shada" title="Jeremy Shada">Jeremy Shada</a>) and his best friend and adoptive brother <a href="/wiki/Jake_the_Dog" title="Jake the Dog">Jake</a> (<a href="/wiki/John_DiMaggio" title="John DiMaggio">John DiMaggio</a>)—a dog with the power to change size and shape at will. Finn and Jake live in the post-apocalyptic Land of Ooo, where they interact with <a href="/wiki/Princess_Bubblegum" title="Princess Bubblegum">Princess Bubblegum</a> (<a href="/wiki/Hynden_Walch" title="Hynden Walch">Hynden Walch</a>), the <a href="/wiki/Ice_King" title="Ice King">Ice King</a> (<a href="/wiki/Tom_Kenny" title="Tom Kenny">Tom Kenny</a>), <a href="/wiki/Marceline_the_Vampire_Queen" title="Marceline the Vampire Queen">Marceline</a> (<a href="/wiki/Olivia_Olson" title="Olivia Olson">Olivia Olson</a>), <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/BMO_(character)" title="BMO (character)">BMO</a> (<a href="/wiki/Niki_Yang" title="Niki Yang">Niki Yang</a>), and others. The series is based on a 2007 <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_(short_film)" title="Adventure Time (short film)">short film</a> that aired on <a href="/wiki/Nicktoons_(American_TV_channel)" title="Nicktoons (American TV channel)">Nicktoons</a>. After the short became a <a href="/wiki/Viral_video" title="Viral video">viral hit</a> on the Internet, <a href="/wiki/Nickelodeon" title="Nickelodeon">Nickelodeon</a>'s executives passed on its option before Cartoon Network commissioned a full-length series from <a href="/wiki/Fred_Seibert" title="Fred Seibert">Fred Seibert</a> and Ward, which was previewed on March 11, 2010. The same year, the series premiered on Cartoon Network on April 5, and it ended its eight-year run on September 3, 2018.
</p><p>The series drew inspiration from a variety of sources, including the fantasy <a href="/wiki/Role-playing_game" title="Role-playing game">role-playing game</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Dungeons_%26_Dragons" title="Dungeons &amp; Dragons">Dungeons &amp; Dragons</a></i> and video games. It was produced using hand-drawn animation; action and dialogue for <a href="/wiki/List_of_Adventure_Time_episodes" title="List of Adventure Time episodes">episodes</a> were decided by <a href="/wiki/Storyboard_artist" title="Storyboard artist">storyboard artists</a> based on rough outlines. Because each episode took roughly eight to nine months to complete, multiple episodes were worked on concurrently. The cast members recorded their lines in group recordings, and the series regularly employed guest actors for minor and recurring characters. Each episode runs for about eleven minutes; pairs of episodes are often telecast to fill half-hour program slots. Cartoon Network announced on September 29, 2016, that the series would conclude in 2018, after the airing of its tenth season. The <a href="/wiki/Come_Along_with_Me_(Adventure_Time)" title="Come Along with Me (Adventure Time)">series finale</a> aired on September 3, 2018, which was followed by the <i><a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time:_Distant_Lands" title="Adventure Time: Distant Lands">Adventure Time: Distant Lands</a></i> specials and the <i><a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time:_Fionna_and_Cake" title="Adventure Time: Fionna and Cake">Adventure Time: Fionna and Cake</a></i> spin-off, which were released on <a href="/wiki/Max_(streaming_service)" title="Max (streaming service)">Max</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-11"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>d<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As of June 2024, two additional spin-offs, entitled <i>Adventure Time: Side Quests</i> and <i>Adventure Time: Heyo BMO</i>, have also been greenlit by Cartoon Network Studios.
</p><p><i>Adventure Time</i> was a ratings success for Cartoon Network, with some of its episodes attracting over three million viewers, and despite being aimed primarily at children, the show has developed a following among teenagers and adults. <i>Adventure Time</i> has received universal acclaim from critics, with much praise for its originality and <a href="/wiki/Worldbuilding" title="Worldbuilding">worldbuilding</a>. The show won eight <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award" title="Primetime Emmy Award">Primetime Emmy Awards</a>, a <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Peabody_Award" title="Peabody Award">Peabody Award</a>, three <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Annie_Award" title="Annie Award">Annie Awards</a>, two <a href="/wiki/British_Academy_Children%27s_Awards" title="British Academy Children's Awards">British Academy Children's Awards</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Motion_Picture_Sound_Editors" title="Motion Picture Sound Editors">Motion Picture Sound Editors Award</a>, and a <a href="/wiki/Kerrang!_Awards" title="Kerrang! Awards"><i>Kerrang!</i> Award</a>. The series has also been nominated for three <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Critics%27_Choice_Television_Award" title="Critics' Choice Television Award">Critics' Choice Television Awards</a>, two <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Annecy_International_Animated_Film_Festival" title="Annecy International Animated Film Festival">Annecy Festival Awards</a>, a <a href="/wiki/TCA_Awards" title="TCA Awards">TCA Award</a>, and a <a href="/wiki/Sundance_Film_Festival" title="Sundance Film Festival">Sundance Film Festival Award</a>, among others. Of the many comic book spin-offs based on the series, one received an <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Eisner_Award" title="Eisner Award">Eisner Award</a> and two <a href="/wiki/Harvey_Awards" title="Harvey Awards">Harvey Awards</a>. The series has also spawned various forms of <a href="/wiki/Brand_licensing" title="Brand licensing">licensed merchandise</a>, including books, video games and clothing.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Premise">Premise</h2></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1236090951" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"><div class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" role="note">Further information: <a href="/wiki/List_of_Adventure_Time_characters" title="List of Adventure Time characters">List of <i>Adventure Time</i> characters</a></div>
<p><i>Adventure Time</i> follows the adventures of a boy named <a href="/wiki/Finn_the_Human" title="Finn the Human">Finn the Human</a> (voiced by <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Shada" title="Jeremy Shada">Jeremy Shada</a>), and his best friend and adoptive brother <a href="/wiki/Jake_the_Dog" title="Jake the Dog">Jake the Dog</a> (<a href="/wiki/John_DiMaggio" title="John DiMaggio">John DiMaggio</a>), who has magical powers to change shape and size at will. <a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Ward" title="Pendleton Ward">Pendleton Ward</a>, the series' creator, describes Finn as a "fiery little kid with strong morals".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-0"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Jake, on the other hand, is based on Tripper Harrison, <a href="/wiki/Bill_Murray" title="Bill Murray">Bill Murray</a>'s character in <i><a href="/wiki/Meatballs_(film)" title="Meatballs (film)">Meatballs</a></i>. This means that while Jake is somewhat carefree, he will "sit [Finn] down and give him some decent advice if he really needs it".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-1"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Finn and Jake live in the post-apocalyptic Land of Ooo, which was ravaged by a cataclysmic event known as the "Mushroom War", a <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Nuclear_war" title="Nuclear war">nuclear war</a> that destroyed civilization a thousand years before the series' events. Throughout the series, Finn and Jake interact with major characters, including <a href="/wiki/Princess_Bubblegum" title="Princess Bubblegum">Princess Bubblegum</a> (<a href="/wiki/Hynden_Walch" title="Hynden Walch">Hynden Walch</a>), the sovereign of the Candy Kingdom and a sentient piece of <a href="/wiki/Chewing_gum" title="Chewing gum">gum</a>; the <a href="/wiki/Ice_King" title="Ice King">Ice King</a> (<a href="/wiki/Tom_Kenny" title="Tom Kenny">Tom Kenny</a>), a menacing but largely misunderstood ice wizard; <a href="/wiki/Marceline_the_Vampire_Queen" title="Marceline the Vampire Queen">Marceline the Vampire Queen</a> (<a href="/wiki/Olivia_Olson" title="Olivia Olson">Olivia Olson</a>), a thousand-year-old vampire and <a href="/wiki/Rock_music" title="Rock music">rock music</a> enthusiast; <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Lumpy_Space_Princess" title="Lumpy Space Princess">Lumpy Space Princess</a> (Pendleton Ward), a melodramatic and immature princess made out of "lumps"; <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/BMO_(character)" title="BMO (character)">BMO</a> (<a href="/wiki/Niki_Yang" title="Niki Yang">Niki Yang</a>), a sentient video game console-shaped <a href="/wiki/Robot" title="Robot">robot</a> that lives with Finn and Jake; and <a href="/wiki/List_of_Adventure_Time_characters#Flame_Princess" title="List of Adventure Time characters">Flame Princess</a> (<a href="/wiki/Jessica_DiCicco" title="Jessica DiCicco">Jessica DiCicco</a>), a flame <a href="/wiki/Elemental" title="Elemental">elemental</a> and ruler of the Fire Kingdom.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-toons_13-0"><a href="#cite_note-toons-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 346">: 346 </span></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-candyland_14-0"><a href="#cite_note-candyland-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-characters_15-0"><a href="#cite_note-characters-15"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Development">Development</h2></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Concept_and_creation">Concept and creation</h3></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1236090951" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"><div class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" role="note">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_(short_film)" title="Adventure Time (short film)">Adventure Time (short film)</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a class="mw-file-description" href="/wiki/File:Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg"><img class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="1246" data-file-width="955" decoding="async" height="261" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg/250px-Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg/330px-Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg/500px-Pendleton_Ward_at_the_Tomorrow_Show.jpg 2x" width="200"/></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Ward" title="Pendleton Ward">Pendleton Ward</a>, the creator of the show</figcaption></figure>
<p>According to series creator Pendleton Ward, the show's style was influenced by his time attending the <a href="/wiki/California_Institute_of_the_Arts" title="California Institute of the Arts">California Institute of the Arts</a> (CalArts) and his experiences working as a writer and <a href="/wiki/Storyboard" title="Storyboard">storyboard</a> artist on <i><a href="/wiki/The_Marvelous_Misadventures_of_Flapjack" title="The Marvelous Misadventures of Flapjack">The Marvelous Misadventures of Flapjack</a></i>, a series that ran on Cartoon Network from 2008 until 2010. In an interview with <i><a href="/wiki/Animation_World_Network" title="Animation World Network">Animation World Network</a></i>, Ward said he strove to combine <i>Adventure Time</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s subversive humor with "beautiful" moments, using <a href="/wiki/Hayao_Miyazaki" title="Hayao Miyazaki">Hayao Miyazaki</a>'s film <i><a href="/wiki/My_Neighbor_Totoro" title="My Neighbor Totoro">My Neighbor Totoro</a></i> as inspiration for the latter.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-2"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward has also named <i><a href="/wiki/Home_Movies_(TV_series)" title="Home Movies (TV series)">Home Movies</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Dr._Katz,_Professional_Therapist" title="Dr. Katz, Professional Therapist">Dr. Katz, Professional Therapist</a></i> as influences, largely because both shows are "relaxing" and feature "conversational dialogue that feels natural [and is neither] over the top [nor] cartoony and shrill".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-theawlarticle_16-0"><a href="#cite_note-theawlarticle-16"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series can trace its origin to a seven-minute, stand-alone animated <a href="/wiki/Short_film" title="Short film">short film</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_(short_film)" title="Adventure Time (short film)">same name</a> (this short was later identified as the show's pilot <i>post facto</i>). Produced by <a href="/wiki/Frederator_Studios" title="Frederator Studios">Frederator Studios</a>, the short was created by Ward almost entirely by himself, and its production concluded in early 2006.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-anotherera_17-0"><a href="#cite_note-anotherera-17"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It was first broadcast on <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Nicktoons_Network" title="Nicktoons Network">Nicktoons Network</a> on January 11, 2007,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-anotherera_17-1"><a href="#cite_note-anotherera-17"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-0"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 24">: 24 </span></sup> and was re-broadcast as part of Frederator's anthology show <i><a href="/wiki/Random!_Cartoons" title="Random! Cartoons">Random! Cartoons</a></i> on December 7, 2008.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-timeenter_19-0"><a href="#cite_note-timeenter-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-20"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After its initial release, the video became a <a href="/wiki/Viral_video" title="Viral video">viral hit</a> on the Internet.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-3"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-1"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 25">: 25 </span></sup> Frederator then pitched an <i>Adventure Time</i> series to Nicktoons Network, which rejected it five times.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-0"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-22"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> When Nicktoons' rights to commission a full series expired, Frederator pitched it to other channels.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-2"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 32">: 32 </span></sup> One of the studios that Frederator approached was Cartoon Network, which was interested in producing a full series, but would commit to a deal only if Ward could prove the pilot "wasn't a one-hit wonder".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-1"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rob Sorcher, the chief content officer at Cartoon Network, was influential in getting the network to take a chance on the show; he recognized the series as "something that felt really indie ... comic book-y [and] new".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-3"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 32">: 32 </span></sup>
</p><p>Cartoon Network asked Ward to submit a sample script for their consideration, but Frederator convinced him to rough out a storyboard instead, as "a board would give a better sense of what was on Pen's mind", according to Frederator's vice president Eric Homan.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-2"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward and his college friends <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Patrick_McHale_(cartoonist)" title="Patrick McHale (cartoonist)">Patrick McHale</a> and <a href="/wiki/Adam_Muto" title="Adam Muto">Adam Muto</a> (the former of whom served as a writer, storyboard artist, and creative director for the show during its first few seasons, while the latter served as a storyboard artist and creative director for the show before becoming its showrunner) began developing ideas, all the while concentrating on "keep[ing] the good things about the original short [while also] improv[ing] on" them.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-3"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-4"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 83">: 83 </span></sup> The group's first product was a rough storyboard featuring Finn and Princess Bubblegum going on a spaghetti-supper date.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-4"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Cartoon Network was not happy with this story, and so Ward, McHale, and Muto created a storyboard for the episode "<a href="/wiki/The_Enchiridion!" title="The Enchiridion!">The Enchiridion!</a>", an attempt to emulate the style of the original Nicktoons short. This tactic proved successful, and in September 2008, Cartoon Network approved a first season, which was produced by <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_Studios" title="Cartoon Network Studios">Cartoon Network Studios</a>. "The Enchiridion!" was the first episode to enter into production.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-enchiridion_21-5"><a href="#cite_note-enchiridion-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-begin_23-0"><a href="#cite_note-begin-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-24"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-25"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Ward and his production team began storyboarding episodes and writing plot outlines, but Cartoon Network was still concerned about the direction of the new series. McHale later recalled that during the pitch of an episode titled "Brothers in Insomnia" (which, for various reasons, was scrapped) the room was filled with executives from Cartoon Network. The pitch went well, but the production staff was soon inundated with questions about the stylistic nature of the series. Around this time, Cartoon Network paused the production of the show in an attempt to resolve these creative issues.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-paul_26-0"><a href="#cite_note-paul-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 114">: 114 </span></sup> A number of writers and animators were let go, and in their place, Cartoon Network management hired three veteran animators who had worked on <i><a href="/wiki/SpongeBob_SquarePants" title="SpongeBob SquarePants">SpongeBob SquarePants</a></i>: Derek Drymon (who served as executive producer for the first season of <i>Adventure Time</i>), Merriwether Williams (who served as head story editor for the show's first and second seasons), and <a href="/wiki/Nick_Jennings_(artist)" title="Nick Jennings (artist)">Nick Jennings</a> (who became the series' long-serving art director).<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-paul_26-1"><a href="#cite_note-paul-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 114">: 114 </span></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-5"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 35">: 35 </span></sup> Drymon, in particular, played a key role at this time, ensuring that both Cartoon Network and the show's production crew were on the same creative page.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-paul_26-2"><a href="#cite_note-paul-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 114">: 114 </span></sup> <a href="/wiki/Thurop_Van_Orman" title="Thurop Van Orman">Thurop Van Orman</a>, the creator of <i>The Marvelous Misadventures of Flapjack</i>, was also hired to guide Ward and his staff for the first two seasons.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-6"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 40">: 40 </span></sup> The storyboard for "Prisoners of Love" assuaged many of the fears some Cartoon Network executives had expressed.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-27"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>As production for season one progressed, more artists were brought on board. <a href="/wiki/Ghostshrimp" title="Ghostshrimp">Dan "Ghostshrimp" Bandit</a>, a freelance illustrator who had also written and storyboarded on <i>Flapjack</i>, was hired as the show's lead background designer; Ward told him to create background art that set the show "in a 'Ghostshrimp World<span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-4"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ghosts_28-0"><a href="#cite_note-ghosts-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ghostshrimp designed major locations, including Finn and Jake's home, the Candy Kingdom, and the Ice Kingdom.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ghosts_28-1"><a href="#cite_note-ghosts-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The position of lead character designer was given to Phil Rynda, who held this role for two and a half seasons. The show's lead production crew (which included Ward and McHale) was initially hesitant to bring him on board, but they were soon convinced by director <a href="/wiki/Larry_Leichliter" title="Larry Leichliter">Larry Leichliter</a>, who assured them Rynda was talented and could draw in a variety of styles.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-7"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 47">: 47 </span></sup> With the producers satisfied, Rynda quickly began designing characters that were simple but still fell in line with "Pen's natural aesthetic".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-8"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 83">: 83 </span></sup> Around this time, Rynda and McHale began drafting artistic guidelines for the show, so that its animation style would always be somewhat consistent.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-9"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 48">: 48 </span></sup> With many of the lead production roles filled, Ward turned his attention to choosing storyboard artists for the first season. He assembled a team made up largely of "younger, inexperienced people", many of whom he discovered on the Internet.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-10"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 41">: 41 </span></sup> Many of these individuals had backgrounds in <a href="/wiki/Alternative_comics" title="Alternative comics">indie comics</a>, and Ward has called them "really smart, smartypants people" who were responsible for inserting more idiosyncratic and spiritual ideas into the series.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-29"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>For the show's first four and a half seasons, Ward served as the showrunner. In an interview with <i><a href="/wiki/Rolling_Stone" title="Rolling Stone">Rolling Stone</a></i>, he said he had stepped down from this role sometime during the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_5" title="Adventure Time season 5">fifth season</a>. As a naturally introverted person, he found interacting with and directing people every day to be exhausting. After Ward resigned from the post, Adam Muto became the showrunner. Until late 2014, Ward continued to work on the cartoon as a storyboard artist and storyline writer.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-rollingstoneinterview_30-0"><a href="#cite_note-rollingstoneinterview-30"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After November 2014, he stopped regularly contributing to episode outlines, but still looked over stories, provided occasional input, and continued to storyboard for the series on a limited basis.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-rollingstoneinterview_30-1"><a href="#cite_note-rollingstoneinterview-30"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-31"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-peneps8_32-0"><a href="#cite_note-peneps8-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Production">Production</h3></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Writing_and_storyboarding">Writing and storyboarding</h4></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a class="mw-file-description" href="/wiki/File:The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg"><img alt="The image depicts a group of adults on the red carpet of an award ceremony." class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="3456" data-file-width="5184" decoding="async" height="200" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg/330px-The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg/500px-The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg/960px-The_crew_of_Adventure_Time_at_the_74th_Annual_Peabody_Awards.jpg 2x" width="300"/></a><figcaption>The crew of <i>Adventure Time</i> at the 74th Annual <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Peabody_Award" title="Peabody Award">Peabody Awards</a> in 2014 (<i>From left to right</i>: <a href="/wiki/Kent_Osborne" title="Kent Osborne">Kent Osborne</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tom_Herpich" title="Tom Herpich">Tom Herpich</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Ward" title="Pendleton Ward">Pendleton Ward</a>, <a href="/wiki/Patrick_McHale_(artist)" title="Patrick McHale (artist)">Pat McHale</a>, Betty Ward, <a href="/wiki/Jack_Pendarvis" title="Jack Pendarvis">Jack Pendarvis</a>, Rob Sorcher, Curtis LeLash and <a href="/wiki/Adam_Muto" title="Adam Muto">Adam Muto</a>) </figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a class="mw-file-description" href="/wiki/File:Adventure_time_storyboard.jpg"><img alt="The image depicts two panels filled with cartoon drawings." class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="471" data-file-width="800" decoding="async" height="147" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/45/Adventure_time_storyboard.jpg/250px-Adventure_time_storyboard.jpg" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/45/Adventure_time_storyboard.jpg/500px-Adventure_time_storyboard.jpg 1.5x" width="250"/></a><figcaption>A storyboard panel drawn by <a href="/wiki/Adam_Muto" title="Adam Muto">Adam Muto</a> for the episode "<a href="/wiki/What_Was_Missing" title="What Was Missing">What Was Missing</a>" showing action, dialogue, and sound effects. <i>Adventure Time</i> is a storyboard-driven series. This means the storyboard artists are also the writers, allowing them to draft the dialogue and the action how they see fit.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ward—a self-professed fan of <a href="/wiki/Ambivalence" title="Ambivalence">ambivalent emotions</a>, such as feeling "happy and scared at the same time"—has called the show a "dark comedy".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-usatoday1_33-0"><a href="#cite_note-usatoday1-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He has also cited the fantasy <a href="/wiki/Role-playing_game" title="Role-playing game">role-playing game</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Dungeons_%26_Dragons" title="Dungeons &amp; Dragons">Dungeons &amp; Dragons</a></i>—of which many of the show's writers are devotees—as an inspiration for the show.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-videodungeon_34-0"><a href="#cite_note-videodungeon-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubinterview_35-0"><a href="#cite_note-avclubinterview-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In the United States, the series is rated <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/TV-PG" title="TV-PG">TV-PG</a>;<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-36"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward said he never wanted to push the boundaries of the PG rating, noting in an interview with <a href="/wiki/Art_of_the_Title" title="Art of the Title">Art of the Title</a> that he "never really even thought about the rating ... we don't like stuff that's overly gross. We like cute stuff and nice things".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-0"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward intended the show's world to have a coherent physical logic, and although magic exists in the story, the show's writers tried to create an internal consistency in the characters' interactions with the world.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-awn_12-5"><a href="#cite_note-awn-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-animag_38-0"><a href="#cite_note-animag-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In an interview with <i><a href="/wiki/The_A.V._Club" title="The A.V. Club">The A.V. Club</a></i>, Ward said the show's writing process usually began with the writers telling each other what they had done the previous week to find something humorous to build on. He also said, "A lot of the time, if we're really stuck, we'll start saying everything that comes to our mind, which is usually the worst stuff, and then someone else will think that's terrible but it'll give him a better idea and the ball just starts rolling like that".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubinterview_35-1"><a href="#cite_note-avclubinterview-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Because of the busy schedule of writing and coordinating a television series, the writers did not have time to play <i>Dungeons and Dragons</i>, but they still wrote stories they would "want to be playing D&amp;D with".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubinterview_35-2"><a href="#cite_note-avclubinterview-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Sometimes, the writers and storyboard artists convened and played writing games.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-cscnsp_39-0"><a href="#cite_note-cscnsp-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> One game that was often used is called <a href="/wiki/Exquisite_corpse" title="Exquisite corpse">exquisite corpse</a>; one writer starts a story on a sheet of paper, and another writer tries to finish it.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-cscnsp_39-1"><a href="#cite_note-cscnsp-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-corpseterrible_40-0"><a href="#cite_note-corpseterrible-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> But while a few episodes (such as the fifth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/Puhoy" title="Puhoy">Puhoy</a>" and the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_6" title="Adventure Time season 6">sixth-season</a> episode "<a href="/wiki/Jake_the_Brick" title="Jake the Brick">Jake the Brick</a>") have been generated using this game,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-11"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 258, 260–61">: 258, 260–61 </span></sup> Ward has said that "the ideas are usually terrible".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-corpseterrible_40-1"><a href="#cite_note-corpseterrible-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Former storyboard artist and creative director <a href="/wiki/Cole_Sanchez" title="Cole Sanchez">Cole Sanchez</a> said episode scripts are either created by expanding the good ideas produced by these writing games, or are based on an idea proposed by a storyboard artist in the hope it can be developed into an episode.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-cscnsp_39-2"><a href="#cite_note-cscnsp-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>After the writers pitched stories, the ideas were compiled onto a two-or-three-page outline that contained "the important beats".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-fangoria_41-0"><a href="#cite_note-fangoria-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The episodes were then passed to storyboard artists (often called "boarders"). While many cartoons are based on script pitches to network executives, Cartoon Network allowed <i>Adventure Time</i> to "build their own teams organically" and communicate using storyboards and <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Animatics" title="Animatics">animatics</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-candyland_14-1"><a href="#cite_note-candyland-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rob Sorcher said this novel approach was sanctioned because the company was dealing with "primarily visual people", and that by using storyboards the writers and artists could learn and grow "by actually doing the work".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-candyland_14-2"><a href="#cite_note-candyland-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The storyboard artists generally worked on an episode in pairs, independent from other storyboarders, which, according to freelance writer David Perlmutter in his book <i><a class="extiw" href="//archive.org/details/americatoonsinhi0000perl" title="iarchive:americatoonsinhi0000perl">America Toons In</a></i>, countered creative <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Ennui" title="Ennui">ennui</a> and prevented episodes from being "alike in either content or tone".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-toons_13-1"><a href="#cite_note-toons-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 346">: 346 </span></sup> The storyboard artists were given a week to "thumbnail" (roughly sketch out) a storyboard and fill in the details complete with action, dialogue, and jokes.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-1"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-fangoria_41-1"><a href="#cite_note-fangoria-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The series' showrunner and his creative directors then reviewed the storyboard and made notes. The artists were then given another week to implement the notes and to clean up the episode.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-2"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Storyboard writing and revising usually took up to a month.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-deadlinesskronked_42-0"><a href="#cite_note-deadlinesskronked-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Animation">Animation</h4></div>
