Yuasa</a> <span style="font-size:85%;">(right)</span></div></div></div></div>
<p>Following the writing revisions, voice actors would record their parts for the episodes and an animatic would be compiled to reduce the running time to the necessary 11 minutes. Specialized artists then created prop, character, and background designs.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-deadlinesskronked_42-1"><a href="#cite_note-deadlinesskronked-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-0"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to Rynda, most of this pre-production was done in <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Photoshop" title="Photoshop">Photoshop</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-44"><a href="#cite_note-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> While the episodes' design and coloring was done at <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_Studios" title="Cartoon Network Studios">Cartoon Network Studios</a> in <a href="/wiki/Burbank,_California" title="Burbank, California">Burbank, California</a>, the actual animation was handled in <a href="/wiki/South_Korea" title="South Korea">South Korea</a> by either <a href="/wiki/Rough_Draft_Studios" title="Rough Draft Studios">Rough Draft Korea</a> or <a href="/wiki/Saerom_Animation" title="Saerom Animation">Saerom Animation</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-1"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-12"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 348-49">: 348-49 </span></sup> Animating an episode often took between three and five months.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-deadlinesskronked_42-2"><a href="#cite_note-deadlinesskronked-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-2"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The animation was hand-drawn on paper, which was then digitally composited and painted with <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Digital_ink_and_paint" title="Digital ink and paint">digital ink and paint</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-drawn_45-0"><a href="#cite_note-drawn-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-46"><a href="#cite_note-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Executive producer <a href="/wiki/Fred_Seibert" title="Fred Seibert">Fred Seibert</a> compared the show's animation style to that of <i><a href="/wiki/Felix_the_Cat_(TV_series)" title="Felix the Cat (TV series)">Felix the Cat</a></i> and various <a href="/wiki/Max_Fleischer" title="Max Fleischer">Max Fleischer</a> cartoons, but said its world was equally inspired by "the world of videogames [<i><a href="/wiki/Sic" title="Sic">sic</a></i>]".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-videodungeon_34-1"><a href="#cite_note-videodungeon-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-animag_38-1"><a href="#cite_note-animag-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>While the episodes were being handled in South Korea, the production crew in the U.S. worked on retakes, <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Underscoring" title="Underscoring">music scoring</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Sound_design" title="Sound design">sound design</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-deadlinesskronked_42-3"><a href="#cite_note-deadlinesskronked-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Upon being completed, the animation was sent back to the U.S., at which point the production crew inspected it, looking for mistakes in the animation or "things that didn't animate the way [the staff] intended".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-3"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These problems were then fixed in Korea and the animation was finalized.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-4"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> From story outlining to broadcast, it took between eight and nine months for each episode to be created; because of this, multiple episodes were worked on concurrently.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubinterview_35-3"><a href="#cite_note-avclubinterview-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-deadlinesskronked_42-4"><a href="#cite_note-deadlinesskronked-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-dailybeast_43-5"><a href="#cite_note-dailybeast-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>While a great majority of the series' episodes were animated by Korean animation studios, <i>Adventure Time</i> occasionally featured guest animators and directors. For instance, the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_2" title="Adventure Time season 2">second-season</a> episode "<a href="/wiki/Guardians_of_Sunshine" title="Guardians of Sunshine">Guardians of Sunshine</a>" was partly rendered in 3-D to emulate the style of a video game.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-drawn_45-1"><a href="#cite_note-drawn-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The fifth-season episode "<a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/A_Glitch_is_a_Glitch" title="A Glitch is a Glitch">A Glitch is a Glitch</a>" was written and directed by Irish filmmaker and writer <a href="/wiki/David_OReilly_(artist)" title="David OReilly (artist)">David OReilly</a> and features his distinctive 3-D animation.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-renewfive_47-0"><a href="#cite_note-renewfive-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Animator <a href="/wiki/James_Baxter_(animator)" title="James Baxter (animator)">James Baxter</a> animated select scenes and characters in both the fifth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/James_Baxter_the_Horse" title="James Baxter the Horse">James Baxter the Horse</a>" as well as the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_8" title="Adventure Time season 8">eighth-season</a> episode "Horse &amp; Ball".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-13"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 299">: 299 </span></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-adamtweet2_48-0"><a href="#cite_note-adamtweet2-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The sixth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/Food_Chain_(Adventure_Time)" title="Food Chain (Adventure Time)">Food Chain</a>" was written, storyboarded, and directed by Japanese <a href="/wiki/Anime" title="Anime">anime</a> director <a href="/wiki/Masaaki_Yuasa" title="Masaaki Yuasa">Masaaki Yuasa</a>, and animated entirely by Yuasa's studio <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Science_SARU" title="Science SARU">Science SARU</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-49"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-wondercon2014_50-0"><a href="#cite_note-wondercon2014-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Another sixth-season episode, "<a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Water_Park_Prank" title="Water Park Prank">Water Park Prank</a>", features <a href="/wiki/Flash_animation" title="Flash animation">Flash animation</a> by David Ferguson.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-51"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Stop-motion" title="Stop-motion">stop-motion</a> episode "<a href="/wiki/Bad_Jubies" title="Bad Jubies">Bad Jubies</a>", directed by <a href="/wiki/Kirsten_Lepore" title="Kirsten Lepore">Kirsten Lepore</a>, aired near the middle of the show's <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_7" title="Adventure Time season 7">seventh season</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-52"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-53"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Finally, Alex and Lindsay Small-Butera, noted for their web series <i>Baman Piderman</i>, contributed animation to the eighth-season episode "Beyond the Grotto" and the ninth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/Ketchup_(Adventure_Time)" title="Ketchup (Adventure Time)">Ketchup</a>".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-54"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-55"><a href="#cite_note-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Voice_cast">Voice cast</h4></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1273380762/mw-parser-output/.tmulti" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"/><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:292px;max-width:292px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:146px;max-width:146px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:210px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a class="mw-file-description" href="/wiki/File:Jeremy_Shada_(16485175731).jpg"><img alt="" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="1592" data-file-width="1088" decoding="async" height="211" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Jeremy_Shada_%2816485175731%29.jpg/250px-Jeremy_Shada_%2816485175731%29.jpg" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Jeremy_Shada_%2816485175731%29.jpg/330px-Jeremy_Shada_%2816485175731%29.jpg 2x" width="144"/></a></span></div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:142px;max-width:142px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:210px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a class="mw-file-description" href="/wiki/File:John_DiMaggio_(49076260988).jpg"><img alt="" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="951" data-file-width="636" decoding="async" height="209" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/John_DiMaggio_%2849076260988%29.jpg/250px-John_DiMaggio_%2849076260988%29.jpg" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/John_DiMaggio_%2849076260988%29.jpg/330px-John_DiMaggio_%2849076260988%29.jpg 2x" width="140"/></a></span></div></div></div><div class="trow" style="display:flex"><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Shada" title="Jeremy Shada">Jeremy Shada</a> (<i>left</i>) and <a href="/wiki/John_DiMaggio" title="John DiMaggio">John DiMaggio</a> (<i>right</i>) star in the series, voicing Finn and Jake, respectively.</div></div></div></div>
<p>The series' voice actors include <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Shada" title="Jeremy Shada">Jeremy Shada</a> (Finn the Human), <a href="/wiki/John_DiMaggio" title="John DiMaggio">John DiMaggio</a> (Jake the Dog), <a href="/wiki/Tom_Kenny" title="Tom Kenny">Tom Kenny</a> (The Ice King), <a href="/wiki/Hynden_Walch" title="Hynden Walch">Hynden Walch</a> (Princess Bubblegum), and <a href="/wiki/Olivia_Olson" title="Olivia Olson">Olivia Olson</a> (Marceline the Vampire Queen). Ward voices several minor characters and Lumpy Space Princess. Former storyboard artist <a href="/wiki/Niki_Yang" title="Niki Yang">Niki Yang</a> voices the sentient video game console BMO in English, as well as Jake's girlfriend <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Lady_Rainicorn" title="Lady Rainicorn">Lady Rainicorn</a> in Korean. Polly Lou Livingston, a friend of Ward's mother Bettie Ward, voices the small elephant <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Tree_Trunks" title="Tree Trunks">Tree Trunks</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-toons_13-2"><a href="#cite_note-toons-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 346">: 346 </span></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-pollylou_56-0"><a href="#cite_note-pollylou-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The <i>Adventure Time</i> cast members recorded their lines together at group recording sessions rather than individually, with the aim of recording natural-sounding dialogue.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-57"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Hynden Walch has described these group recordings as akin to "doing a play reading—a really, really out there play".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Cast_58-0"><a href="#cite_note-Cast-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The series regularly employed guest actors for minor and recurring characters,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-59"><a href="#cite_note-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and crew members cast people with whom they were interested in working. For instance, in a panel, Muto and <a href="/wiki/Kent_Osborne" title="Kent Osborne">Kent Osborne</a> said the <i>Adventure Time</i> crew often sought out actors who had had roles in the television programs <i><a href="/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation" title="Star Trek: The Next Generation">Star Trek: The Next Generation</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Office_(American_TV_series)" title="The Office (American TV series)">The Office</a></i> to play various supporting or background characters.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-60"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Title_sequence_and_music">Title sequence and music</h4></div>
<p>When Ward was developing the series' title sequences, the rough draft version consisted of quick shots and vignettes that were "just sort of crazy [and] nonsensical", which alluded to the show's theme of quirky adventures.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-3"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These drafts included "the characters ... just punching random ghosts and monsters, jumping through anything and everything [and] there were a bunch of atomic bombs at the end of it".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-4"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward later called this version "really silly".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-5"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He sent the draft to Cartoon Network; they did not like it and wanted something more graphical like the introduction to <i><a href="/wiki/The_Brady_Bunch" title="The Brady Bunch">The Brady Bunch</a></i>. Inspired by the title sequences of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Simpsons" title="The Simpsons">The Simpsons</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Pee-wee%27s_Playhouse" title="Pee-wee's Playhouse">Pee-wee's Playhouse</a></i>, Ward developed a new title sequence featuring a panning sweep of the Land of Ooo while a synthesizer note rose slowly until the main theme was played. Ward's draft for this idea was handed to layout animators, who then finalized the timing for the sequence. From there, the sequence evolved; while Ward added "silly character stuff", Patrick McHale focused his attention on the Ice King's shot and gave him a "high school [year]book" smile. The crew also struggled to get the shadows in the shot featuring Marceline correct.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-6"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After the panning sweep, the sequence cuts to the theme song, which plays while shots of Finn and Jake adventuring are shown. For this part of the sequence, Ward was inspired by the "simple" aspects of the introduction to the 2007 comedy film <i><a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Superbad_(film)" title="Superbad (film)">Superbad</a></i>. When the theme mentions "Jake the Dog" and "Finn the Human", the characters' names are displayed next to their heads, with a solid color in the background.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-7"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The sequence was finalized immediately before the series aired.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-8"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The show's eponymous theme song is sung by Ward, accompanied by a <a href="/wiki/Ukulele" title="Ukulele">ukulele</a>. It is first heard in the pilot episode; in that version, Ward is accompanied by an acoustic guitar. For the version used in the series, Ward sang in a higher register to match the ukulele's range.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-9"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The theme song's final version was originally supposed to be a <a href="/wiki/Temp_track" title="Temp track">temporary version</a>. Ward said, "I recorded the lyrics for the opening title in the animatics room where we have this little crummy microphone just so that we could add it to the titles and submit it to the network. Later, we tried re-recording it and I didn't like it ... I only liked the temp one!"<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-10"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Because the series' finalized theme song was originally recorded as a temp track, ambient noises can be heard throughout. For instance, the sound of Derek Drymon typing can be heard while Jake is walking through the Ice Kingdom. According to Ward, much of the series' music has similar "hiss and grit" because one of the show's original composers, Casey James Basichis, "lives in a pirate ship he's built inside of an apartment [and] you can hear floorboards squeak and lots of other weird sounds".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-aotmusicrev_37-11"><a href="#cite_note-aotmusicrev-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As the show progressed, Basichis's friend Tim Kiefer joined the show as an additional composer.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-61"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The two now work together on its music.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-music_62-0"><a href="#cite_note-music-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The show's title sequence and theme song have stayed mostly consistent throughout its run, with seven exceptions. During the episodes featuring <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Fionna_Campbell_(character)" title="Fionna Campbell (character)">Fionna Campbell</a> and <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Cake_the_Cat" title="Cake the Cat">Cake the Cat</a> (<a href="/wiki/Viz." title="Viz.">viz.</a> <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_3" title="Adventure Time season 3">season three</a>'s "<a href="/wiki/Fionna_and_Cake_(episode)" title="Fionna and Cake (episode)">Fionna and Cake</a>", season five's "<a href="/wiki/Bad_Little_Boy" title="Bad Little Boy">Bad Little Boy</a>", season six's "The Prince Who Wanted Everything", season eight's "Five Short Tables", and <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_9" title="Adventure Time season 9">season nine</a>'s "Fionna and Cake and Fionna") the series runs a different intro sequence that mirrors the original, with the major exception that all the characters are <a href="/wiki/Gender_bender" title="Gender bender">gender-bent</a>, and the theme is sung by former storyboard revisionist <a href="/wiki/Natasha_Allegri" title="Natasha Allegri">Natasha Allegri</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-63"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Likewise, the intro to the series' three miniseries are each unique: the introduction to the Marceline-centric <i><a href="/wiki/Stakes_(miniseries)" title="Stakes (miniseries)">Stakes</a></i> (2015) places most of the emphasis on Marceline, and the theme song is sung by Olson;<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ew.comseason7_64-0"><a href="#cite_note-ew.comseason7-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> the introduction to <i><a href="/wiki/Islands_(miniseries)" title="Islands (miniseries)">Islands</a></i> (2017) adopts a nautical theme, highlights the principal characters in the miniseries, and is sung by Shada;<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-tumblrtitleseason8_65-0"><a href="#cite_note-tumblrtitleseason8-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and the intro to <i><a href="/wiki/Elements_(miniseries)" title="Elements (miniseries)">Elements</a></i> (2017) features imagery reflecting the four primary elements in the <i>Adventure Time</i> universe (that is: fire, ice, slime, and candy) and is sung by Hynden Walch.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-66"><a href="#cite_note-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The introductions to the guest-animated episodes "A Glitch Is a Glitch" and "Food Chain" are each unique, featuring animation courtesy of OReilly and Yuasa, respectively.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-67"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-68"><a href="#cite_note-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Finally, the series finale, "Come Along With Me", features an introduction offering viewers a glimpse of future Ooo, 1,000 years after Finn and Jake. This intro features the new characters Shermy and Beth and is sung by the latter (voiced by <a href="/wiki/Willow_Smith" title="Willow Smith">Willow Smith</a>).<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-69"><a href="#cite_note-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series regularly features songs and musical numbers. Many of the cast members—including Shada, Kenny, and Olson—sing their characters' songs.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Cast_58-1"><a href="#cite_note-Cast-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-voicejeremyfinn_70-0"><a href="#cite_note-voicejeremyfinn-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-71"><a href="#cite_note-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Characters often express their emotions in song; examples of this include Marceline's song "I'm Just Your Problem" (from season three's "<a href="/wiki/What_Was_Missing" title="What Was Missing">What Was Missing</a>") and Finn's "All Gummed Up Inside" (from season three's "<a href="/wiki/Incendium" title="Incendium">Incendium</a>").<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-72"><a href="#cite_note-72"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-73"><a href="#cite_note-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> While the series' background music is composed by Basichis and Kiefer, the songs sung by characters are often written by the storyboard artists.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-74"><a href="#cite_note-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-fryptich_75-0"><a href="#cite_note-fryptich-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> And while it is a general rarity, the show also occasionally refers to <a href="/wiki/Pop_music" title="Pop music">popular music</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-76"><a href="#cite_note-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Early during the show's run, Frederator, Seibert's production company, occasionally uploaded demos and full versions of songs sung by the characters to their official website,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-77"><a href="#cite_note-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and when the production crew set up a series <a href="/wiki/Tumblr" title="Tumblr">Tumblr</a> account, this tradition of publishing demos and full versions of songs to the public was revived.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-78"><a href="#cite_note-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On November 20, 2015, the label Spacelab9 released a limited-edition 12" <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Long_play" title="Long play">LP</a> featuring many of Marceline's songs,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-79"><a href="#cite_note-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> followed by a <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/The_Music_of_Ooo" title="The Music of Ooo">38-song series soundtrack</a> in October 2016.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-80"><a href="#cite_note-80"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Setting_and_mythology">Setting and mythology</h4></div>
<p>The show is set in the fictional "Land of Ooo", in a post-apocalyptic future about a thousand years after a <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_holocaust" title="Nuclear holocaust">nuclear holocaust</a> called the "Great Mushroom War".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-artooo_18-14"><a href="#cite_note-artooo-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 78">: 78 </span></sup> According to Ward, the show takes place "after the bombs have fallen and magic has come back into the world".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-81"><a href="#cite_note-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Before the series was fully developed, Ward intended the Land of Ooo to simply be "magical". After the production of the episode "Business Time", in which an iceberg containing reanimated businessmen floats to the surface of a lake, the show became explicitly post-apocalyptic; Ward said the production crew "just ran with it".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-usatoday1_33-1"><a href="#cite_note-usatoday1-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward later described the setting as "candyland on the surface and dark underneath",<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-candyland_14-3"><a href="#cite_note-candyland-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> noting he had never intended the Mushroom War and the post-apocalyptic elements to be "hit over the head in the show".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-io09interview_82-0"><a href="#cite_note-io09interview-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He limited it to "cars buried underground in the background [and other elements that do not] raise any eyebrows".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-io09interview_82-1"><a href="#cite_note-io09interview-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward has said the series' post-apocalyptic elements were influenced by the 1979 film <i><a href="/wiki/Mad_Max_(film)" title="Mad Max (film)">Mad Max</a></i>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-usatoday1_33-2"><a href="#cite_note-usatoday1-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Kenny called the way the elements are worked into the plot "very fill-in-the-blanks", and DiMaggio said, "it's been obvious the Land of Ooo has some issues".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-io09interview_82-2"><a href="#cite_note-io09interview-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series has a <a href="/wiki/Canon_(fiction)" title="Canon (fiction)">canonical</a> <a href="/wiki/Mythology_(fiction)" title="Mythology (fiction)">mythology</a>—or, an overarching plot and backstory—that is expanded upon in various episodes.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-indiemyth_83-0"><a href="#cite_note-indiemyth-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-io9myth_84-0"><a href="#cite_note-io9myth-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This mythology mainly involves the nature of the Mushroom War, the origin of the series' principal antagonist the Lich, and the backstories of several of the series' principal and recurring characters.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-indiemyth_83-1"><a href="#cite_note-indiemyth-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-io9myth_84-1"><a href="#cite_note-io9myth-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclub_85-0"><a href="#cite_note-avclub-85"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ward once noted that the details behind the Mushroom War and the series' dark mythology form "a story worth telling", but he also felt the show would be better off if the show "dance[d] around how heavy the back-history of Ooo is".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-86"><a href="#cite_note-86"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="LGBTQ+_representation"><span id="LGBTQ.2B_representation"></span>LGBTQ+ representation</h3></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1236090951" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"/><div class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" role="note">See also: <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_and_LGBT_representation" title="Cartoon Network and LGBT representation">Cartoon Network and LGBT representation</a></div>
<p>After the September 2011 episode "<a href="/wiki/What_Was_Missing" title="What Was Missing">What Was Missing</a>" hinted at romantic subtext between Marceline and Bubblegum, fans began to <a href="/wiki/Shipping_(fandom)" title="Shipping (fandom)">"ship"</a> the two, referring to the pairing as "Bubbline".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-nichbrit2011_87-0"><a href="#cite_note-nichbrit2011-87"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Ewart_88-0"><a href="#cite_note-Ewart-88"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Some reviewers also discussed the possible relationship, with Kjerstin Johnson of <i><a href="/wiki/Bitch_(magazine)" title="Bitch (magazine)">Bitch</a></i> magazine expressing hope that that show's "queer cartoon subtext" would turn into "a queer cartoon subplot".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-johkje2011_89-0"><a href="#cite_note-johkje2011-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Rude2014_90-0"><a href="#cite_note-Rude2014-90"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eventually, Bubblegum and Marceline's relationship was confirmed in the series finale, "<a href="/wiki/Come_Along_with_Me_(Adventure_Time)" title="Come Along with Me (Adventure Time)">Come Along With Me</a>", which also featured the two characters kissing.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-buzzfeedolson_91-0"><a href="#cite_note-buzzfeedolson-91"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Adegoke_92-0"><a href="#cite_note-Adegoke-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> While Bubblegum seems to have dated a male character named Mr. Cream Puff,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-93"><a href="#cite_note-93"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> her exact sexuality, unlike Marceline's,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Moen_94-0"><a href="#cite_note-Moen-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> has not been confirmed. As such, reviewers have argued that she is either bisexual,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-95"><a href="#cite_note-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> non-binary,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Syfy_96-0"><a href="#cite_note-Syfy-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> queer,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Syfy_96-1"><a href="#cite_note-Syfy-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> lesbian,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-97"><a href="#cite_note-97"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> or a combination of some of the latter, as both live in a world where "<a href="/wiki/Sexual_fluidity" title="Sexual fluidity">sexuality is somewhat fluid</a>."<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-98"><a href="#cite_note-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Much of the series' LGBTQ+ representation was the result of storyboard artist <a href="/wiki/Rebecca_Sugar" title="Rebecca Sugar">Rebecca Sugar</a>, who soon after joining the production crew "became more aware of what we're really saying by excluding [LGBTQ] characters" from children's TV—a situation which felt "more and more dire" to her.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Romano2018_99-0"><a href="#cite_note-Romano2018-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> She thus began working hard to put "LGBTQIA characters in G-rated content" in the years to follow.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Romano2018_99-1"><a href="#cite_note-Romano2018-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zeroing in on the relationship between Marceline and Bubblegum, Sugar tried to foster their relationship.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-100"><a href="#cite_note-100"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Bust_101-0"><a href="#cite_note-Bust-101"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In a March 2021 <i><a href="/wiki/Vanity_Fair_(magazine)" title="Vanity Fair (magazine)">Vanity Fair</a></i> interview, Sugar said that she was encouraged by the "creative team to put their own life experiences into the character of Marceline," but when this led to a "romantic storyline between Marceline and Princess Bubblegum", <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a> executives intervened. This moment led Sugar and the rest of the show's team to see the limit of what they could accomplish, in terms of representation.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-102"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The writers initially responded to this roadblock by working queer themes into episodes as subtext to avoid controversy or network censorship, but later episodes would openly expand on these themes, bringing them to the forefront of the series' plot.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-paul_26-3"><a href="#cite_note-paul-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 43-51">: 43-51 </span></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Moen_94-1"><a href="#cite_note-Moen-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-103"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Finale">Finale</h3></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1236090951" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"/><div class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" role="note">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Come_Along_with_Me_(Adventure_Time)" title="Come Along with Me (Adventure Time)">Come Along with Me (<i>Adventure Time</i>)</a></div>
<p>During the last seasons of <i>Adventure Time</i>, there was talk at Cartoon Network about concluding the series. <a href="/wiki/Olivia_Olson" title="Olivia Olson">Olivia Olson</a>, who provided the voice of Marceline, said that since this discussion wore on for a while and "the ending of the show was getting stretched and stretched and stretched".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-latimesend_104-0"><a href="#cite_note-latimesend-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Chief content officer <a href="/wiki/Rob_Sorcher" title="Rob Sorcher">Rob Sorcher</a> told the <i><a href="/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times" title="Los Angeles Times">Los Angeles Times</a></i> of the network's decision to end the series, saying:
</p>
<blockquote><p><i>Adventure Time</i> was playing less and less on Cartoon Network, yet we were moving towards a large volume of episodes. And I really began thinking "[The end] can't come quickly as a sudden company decision, it needs to be a conversation over a period of time." And it did also strike me that if we don't wind this up soon, we're going to have a generation of fans graduate through the [television] demo[graphic that Cartoon Network targets] and we won't have completed a thought for them.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-latimesend_104-1"><a href="#cite_note-latimesend-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Consequently, on September 29, 2016, Cartoon Network confirmed that the series would conclude after its tenth season.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-kentfinale_105-0"><a href="#cite_note-kentfinale-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The final episode of the series is a special, titled "Come Along with Me"; the special was written and storyboarded by <a href="/wiki/Tom_Herpich" title="Tom Herpich">Tom Herpich</a>, <a href="/wiki/Steve_Wolfhard" title="Steve Wolfhard">Steve Wolfhard</a>, Seo Kim, Somvilay Xayaphone, Hanna K. Nyström, Aleks Sennwald, and Sam Alden, and <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Graham_Falk" title="Graham Falk">Graham Falk</a>. The story was developed by Herpich, Wolfhard, <a href="/wiki/Ashly_Burch" title="Ashly Burch">Ashly Burch</a>, showrunner <a href="/wiki/Adam_Muto" title="Adam Muto">Adam Muto</a>, head writer <a href="/wiki/Kent_Osborne" title="Kent Osborne">Kent Osborne</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jack_Pendarvis" title="Jack Pendarvis">Jack Pendarvis</a>, <a href="/wiki/Julia_Pott" title="Julia Pott">Julia Pott</a>, and series creator <a href="/wiki/Pendleton_Ward" title="Pendleton Ward">Pendleton Ward</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-seriesfinale_106-0"><a href="#cite_note-seriesfinale-106"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Former head background designer <a href="/wiki/Ghostshrimp" title="Ghostshrimp">Ghostshrimp</a> returned after having officially left the series during the <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_4" title="Adventure Time season 4">fourth season</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ghostshrimpface_107-0"><a href="#cite_note-ghostshrimpface-107"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>According to Osborne, Cartoon Network provided the writers with "an opportunity to spend a lot of time thinking about the finale" before production ended.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-kentfinale_105-1"><a href="#cite_note-kentfinale-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In an interview with <i><a href="/wiki/TV_Guide" title="TV Guide">TV Guide</a></i>, Muto explained that the show's writers used many of the episodes preceding the finale to conclude minor character story arcs "so we wouldn't have to cram too much in at the very end here."<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-tvg_108-0"><a href="#cite_note-tvg-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This allowed the finale itself to be "less dense" by simply "hitting the big [beats] and then finding vignettes for all the characters ... so we could get snapshots of where they could end up."<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-tvg_108-1"><a href="#cite_note-tvg-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to Pendarvis, storyline writing for the series ended in mid-November 2016,<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-stylus_109-0"><a href="#cite_note-stylus-109"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> with the last storyline meeting held on November 21.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-finalmeetingtweet_110-0"><a href="#cite_note-finalmeetingtweet-110"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A tweet by Osborne revealed that the series' final script was pitched to storyboarders, with Alden and Nyström in attendance, on November 28.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-kenttweet_111-0"><a href="#cite_note-kenttweet-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-samlast_112-0"><a href="#cite_note-samlast-112"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-hannalast_113-0"><a href="#cite_note-hannalast-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This episode was then pitched to the show's producers during the third week of December 2016.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-insta-sam_114-0"><a href="#cite_note-insta-sam-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-mutotweet_115-0"><a href="#cite_note-mutotweet-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Voice recording for the episode ended on January 31, 2017, as confirmed by a number of cast members, including <a href="/wiki/Maria_Bamford" title="Maria Bamford">Maria Bamford</a> and <a href="/wiki/Andy_Milonakis" title="Andy Milonakis">Andy Milonakis</a>. The series finale aired on September 3, 2018 to largely positive reception.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ew_116-0"><a href="#cite_note-ew-116"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ign_117-0"><a href="#cite_note-ign-117"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-overlyanimatedreview_118-0"><a href="#cite_note-overlyanimatedreview-118"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avc_119-0"><a href="#cite_note-avc-119"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Broadcast_and_ratings">Broadcast and ratings</h2></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Episodes">Episodes</h3></div>
<link href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1236090951" rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style"/><div class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" role="note">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_Adventure_Time_episodes" title="List of Adventure Time episodes">List of <i>Adventure Time</i> episodes</a></div>
<p>Each <i>Adventure Time</i> episode is about eleven minutes in length; pairs of episodes are often telecast in order to fill a half-hour program time slot.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-120"><a href="#cite_note-120"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Before the official debut of the first season, Cartoon Network aired both "Business Time" and "<a href="/wiki/Evicted!" title="Evicted!">Evicted!</a>" on March 11 and 18, respectively, advertising these showings as "previews" of the series-to-come.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-preview_business_121-0"><a href="#cite_note-preview_business-121"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-122"><a href="#cite_note-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The show officially debuted with "Slumber Party Panic" on April 5, 2010.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-LATimesReview_123-0"><a href="#cite_note-LATimesReview-123"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During the latter part of its run, the show began to experiment with the <a href="/wiki/Miniseries" title="Miniseries">miniseries</a> format. The first of these was <i>Stakes</i> (2015), which aired during the show's seventh season. The following miniseries, <i>Islands</i> (2017) aired as part of the eighth season. The third and final miniseries, <i>Elements</i> (2017), aired during the show's ninth season.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Staff_writers_2015_124-0"><a href="#cite_note-Staff_writers_2015-124"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-125"><a href="#cite_note-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-polygonnews_126-0"><a href="#cite_note-polygonnews-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The show's <a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time_season_7" title="Adventure Time season 7">seventh season</a> was originally intended to comprise 39 episodes, ranging from "Bonnie &amp; Neddy" to "Reboot". However, when it came time to upload the season onto streaming sites like CartoonNetwork.com, <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network" title="Cartoon Network">Cartoon Network</a> chose to end the season with the episode "The Thin Yellow Line", for a total of 26 episodes. This new episode count for the season was cemented by the release of the complete seventh season <a href="/wiki/DVD-Video" title="DVD-Video">DVD</a> on July 18, 2017, which included episodes "Bonnie &amp; Neddy" through "The Thin Yellow Line".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-paul_26-4"><a href="#cite_note-paul-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 159">: 159 </span></sup> As such, the episode and season number sequence is accordingly changed, as follows:
</p>

</div>
<p>For its first six seasons, episodes regularly aired once a week. Starting in November 2014, the show began to air new episodes via "bombs", or weeks in which new episodes debuted every day.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-thanksgivingschedule_132-0"><a href="#cite_note-thanksgivingschedule-132"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This change in airing style disrupted the viewing patterns of some fans, as Dave Trumbore of <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Collider_(website)" title="Collider (website)">Collider</a> explained: "Back when [the show] was regularly airing in a more traditional schedule, it was a little easier to keep track of the completely insane episodes full of half-explained mythology and lots and lots of non-sequiturs. During the last few seasons, however, [when] the episodes started to arrive in more of a scattershot fashion scheduled around multi-part specials [it became easier to miss] the random airings of certain episodes".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-133"><a href="#cite_note-133"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series' initial run concluded in 2018, after the airing of its tenth season.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-finaleforgood_134-0"><a href="#cite_note-finaleforgood-134"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Reruns have aired on <a href="/wiki/Boomerang_(TV_network)" title="Boomerang (TV network)">Boomerang</a> and <a href="/wiki/Adult_Swim" title="Adult Swim">Adult Swim</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-135"><a href="#cite_note-135"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-136"><a href="#cite_note-136"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Ratings">Ratings</h3></div>
<p>Upon its debut, <i>Adventure Time</i> was a ratings success for Cartoon Network. In March 2013, it was reported that the show averaged roughly 2 to 3 million viewers an episode.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-timeenter_19-1"><a href="#cite_note-timeenter-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to a 2012 report by <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Nielsen_ratings" title="Nielsen ratings">Nielsen</a>, the show consistently ranked first in its time slot among boys aged 2–14.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-candyland_14-4"><a href="#cite_note-candyland-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The show premiered on April 5, 2010, and was watched by 2.5 million viewers.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-firstep_137-0"><a href="#cite_note-firstep-137"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The episode was a ratings success. According to a press release by Cartoon Network, the episode's time slot saw triple-digit percentage increases from the previous year. The program was viewed by 1.661 million children aged 2–11, which marked a 110 percent increase from the previous year's figures. It was watched by 837,000 children aged 9–14, a 239 percent increase on the previous year's figures.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-138"><a href="#cite_note-138"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Between the second and sixth seasons, the show's ratings continued to grow; the second-season premiere was watched by 2.001 million viewers, the third-season premiere by 2.686 million, the fourth-season premiere by 2.655 million, the fifth-season premiere by 3.435 million, and the sixth-season premiere by 3.321 million.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-nightratings_139-0"><a href="#cite_note-nightratings-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>135<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-140"><a href="#cite_note-140"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Zap2it_141-0"><a href="#cite_note-Zap2it-141"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-finnjakeseason5ratings_142-0"><a href="#cite_note-finnjakeseason5ratings-142"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>138<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-seasonpremierewakeupescape_143-0"><a href="#cite_note-seasonpremierewakeupescape-143"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>139<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The show's seventh-season opener took a substantial ratings tumble, being watched by only 1.07 million viewers.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-Metcalf,_Mitch_144-0"><a href="#cite_note-Metcalf,_Mitch-144"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>140<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Likewise, the eighth-, ninth-, and tenth-season premieres were watched by only 1.13, 0.71, and 0.77 million viewers, respectively.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-brokerating_145-0"><a href="#cite_note-brokerating-145"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-orbratings_146-0"><a href="#cite_note-orbratings-146"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-fourepisodebomb_147-0"><a href="#cite_note-fourepisodebomb-147"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>143<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The series finale, "Come Along with Me", was viewed by 0.92 million viewers and scored a 0.25 <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Nielsen_rating" title="Nielsen rating">Nielsen rating</a> in the 18- to 49-year-old demographic, which means the episode was seen by 0.25 percent of all individuals aged 18 to 49 years old who were watching television at the time of the episode's airing.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-finaleviewers_148-0"><a href="#cite_note-finaleviewers-148"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>144<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Home_media_and_streaming_service">Home media and streaming service</h3></div>
<p>On September 27, 2011, Cartoon Network released the <a href="/wiki/DVD_region_code#Region_codes_and_countries" title="DVD region code">region 1</a> DVD <i>My Two Favorite People</i>, which features a selection of twelve episodes from the series' first two seasons.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-tvshowdvdlistings_149-0"><a href="#cite_note-tvshowdvdlistings-149"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>145<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-150"><a href="#cite_note-150"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>146<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Following this, several other region-1 compilation DVDs have been released, including: <i>It Came from the Nightosphere</i> (2012), <i>Jake vs. Me-Mow</i> (2012), <i>Fionna and Cake</i> (2013), <i>Jake the Dad</i> (2013), <i>The Suitor</i> (2014), <i>Princess Day</i> (2014), <i>Adventure Time and Friends</i> (2014), <i>Finn the Human</i> (2014), <i>Frost &amp; Fire</i> (2015), <i>The Enchiridion</i> (2015), <i>Stakes</i> (2016), <i>Card Wars</i> (2016), and <i>Islands</i> (2017). All of the seasons have been released on DVD, and the first six have been released domestically on <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc" title="Blu-ray Disc">Blu-ray</a>.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-tvshowdvdlistings_149-1"><a href="#cite_note-tvshowdvdlistings-149"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>145<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-151"><a href="#cite_note-151"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>147<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A box set containing the entire series was released on DVD on April 30, 2019.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-completeseries_152-0"><a href="#cite_note-completeseries-152"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>148<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On March 30, 2013, the first season of <i>Adventure Time</i> was made available on the <a href="/wiki/Netflix" title="Netflix">Netflix</a> Instant Watch service for online streaming; the second season was made available on March 30, 2014.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-153"><a href="#cite_note-153"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>149<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-154"><a href="#cite_note-154"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>150<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Both seasons were removed from Netflix on March 30, 2015.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-155"><a href="#cite_note-155"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>151<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The series was made available for streaming via <a href="/wiki/Hulu" title="Hulu">Hulu</a> on May 1, 2015.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-156"><a href="#cite_note-156"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>152<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>While in the United States, <a href="/wiki/Max_(streaming_service)" title="Max (streaming service)">HBO Max</a> becomes the primary platform to watch <i><a href="/wiki/Adventure_Time:_Distant_Lands" title="Adventure Time: Distant Lands">Adventure Time: Distant Lands</a></i>, there are debuts of "BMO", the first special of the spin-off series, in different countries and regions in respective Cartoon Network channels worldwide, on different dates mainly in 2020; such as October 24 (<a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(Turkish_TV_channel)" title="Cartoon Network (Turkish TV channel)">Turkey</a>),<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-157"><a href="#cite_note-157"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>153<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> October 25 (<a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(French_TV_channel)" title="Cartoon Network (French TV channel)">France</a>),<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-158"><a href="#cite_note-158"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>154<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-159"><a href="#cite_note-159"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>155<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> November 21 (the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">United Kingdom</a>),<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-160"><a href="#cite_note-160"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>156<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> December 12 (<a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(German_TV_channel)" title="Cartoon Network (German TV channel)">Germany</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(Australia_and_New_Zealand)" title="Cartoon Network (Australia and New Zealand)">Australia</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(Asia)" title="Cartoon Network (Asia)">Taiwan</a>),<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-161"><a href="#cite_note-161"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>157<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-162"><a href="#cite_note-162"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>158<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-163"><a href="#cite_note-163"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>159<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-164"><a href="#cite_note-164"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>160<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and December 27 (<a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(Central_and_Eastern_European_TV_channel)" title="Cartoon Network (Central and Eastern European TV channel)">Russia</a>).<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-165"><a href="#cite_note-165"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>161<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In <a href="/wiki/Cartoon_Network_(South_Korea)" title="Cartoon Network (South Korea)">South Korea</a>, the debut was on January 1, 2021.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-166"><a href="#cite_note-166"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Reception">Reception</h2></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Critical_reception">Critical reception</h3></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1224211176">.mw-parser-output .quotebox{background-color:#F9F9F9;border:1px solid #aaa;box-sizing:border-box;padding:10px;font-size:88%;max-width:100%}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft{margin:.5em 1.4em .8em 0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright{margin:.5em 0 .8em 1.4em}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.centered{overflow:hidden;position:relative;margin:.5em auto .8em auto}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft span,.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright span{font-style:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox>blockquote{margin:0;padding:0;border-left:0;font-family:inherit;font-size:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-title{text-align:center;font-size:110%;font-weight:bold}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote>:first-child{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote:last-child>:last-child{margin-bottom:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:before{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" “ ";vertical-align:-45%;line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:after{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" ” ";line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .left-aligned{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .right-aligned{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .center-aligned{text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quote-title,.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quotebox-quote{display:block}.mw-parser-output .quotebox cite{display:block;font-style:normal}@media screen and (max-width:640px){.mw-parser-output .quotebox{width:100%!important;margin:0 0 .8em!important;float:none!important}}</style><div class="quotebox pullquote floatright" style="width:25%; ;">
<blockquote class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style="">
<p>"<i>Adventure Time</i> makes me wish I were a kid again, just so I could grow up to be as awesome as the kids who are currently watching <i>Adventure Time</i> will be".
</p>
</blockquote>
<div style="padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em"><cite class="left-aligned" style=""><i>Entertainment Weekly</i> staff.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ewrev_167-0"><a href="#cite_note-ewrev-167"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>163<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></cite></div>
</div>
<p>The show has received universal acclaim from critics. <i>The A.V. Club</i> reviewer Zack Handlen called it "a terrific show [that] fits beautifully in that gray area between kid and adult entertainment in a way that manages to satisfy both a desire for sophisticated (i.e., weird) writing and plain old silliness".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubpraise_168-0"><a href="#cite_note-avclubpraise-168"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><i>Adventure Time</i> has been complimented for its resemblance to cartoons of the past. In an article for the <i><a href="/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times" title="Los Angeles Times">Los Angeles Times</a></i>, television critic Robert Lloyd compared the series to "the sort of cartoons they made when cartoons themselves were young and delighted in bringing all things to rubbery life".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-LATimesReview_123-1"><a href="#cite_note-LATimesReview-123"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Robert Mclaughlin of <a href="/wiki/Den_of_Geek" title="Den of Geek">Den of Geek</a> expressed a similar sentiment when he wrote that <i>Adventure Time</i> "is the first cartoon in a long time that is pure imagination".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-denogeek_169-0"><a href="#cite_note-denogeek-169"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>165<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He complimented the show for "its non-reliance on continually referencing pop culture".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-denogeek_169-1"><a href="#cite_note-denogeek-169"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>165<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eric Kohn of <i><a href="/wiki/IndieWire" title="IndieWire">IndieWire</a></i> said the show "represents the progress of [cartoon] medium" in the current decade.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-indiewire_170-0"><a href="#cite_note-indiewire-170"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>166<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>A number of reviews have positively compared the series and its creators to other culturally significant works and individuals, respectively. In 2013, <i>Entertainment Weekly</i> reviewer Darren Franich called the series "a hybrid sci-fi/fantasy/horror/musical/fairy tale, with echoes of <i><a href="/wiki/Calvin_and_Hobbes" title="Calvin and Hobbes">Calvin and Hobbes</a></i>, Hayao Miyazaki, <i><a href="/wiki/Final_Fantasy" title="Final Fantasy">Final Fantasy</a></i>, <a href="/wiki/Richard_Linklater" title="Richard Linklater">Richard Linklater</a>, <i><a href="/wiki/Where_the_Wild_Things_Are" title="Where the Wild Things Are">Where the Wild Things Are</a></i>, and the music video you made with your high school garage band".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ewA_171-0"><a href="#cite_note-ewA-171"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>167<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Emily Nussbaum of <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_Yorker" title="The New Yorker">The New Yorker</a></i> praised <i>Adventure Time</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s unique approach to emotion, humor, and philosophy by likening it to "<i><a href="/wiki/World_of_Warcraft" title="World of Warcraft">World of Warcraft</a></i> as recapped by <a href="/wiki/Carl_Jung" title="Carl Jung">Carl Jung</a>".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-172"><a href="#cite_note-172"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>168<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zack Handlen of <i>The A.V. Club</i> concluded that the show was "basically what would happen if you asked a bunch of 12-year-olds to make a cartoon, only it's the best possible version of that, like if all the 12-year-olds were super geniuses and some of them were <a href="/wiki/Stan_Lee" title="Stan Lee">Stan Lee</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jack_Kirby" title="Jack Kirby">Jack Kirby</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Marx_Brothers" title="Marx Brothers">Marx Brothers</a>".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-avclubpraise_168-1"><a href="#cite_note-avclubpraise-168"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><i>Adventure Time</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s willingness to explore dark, sad, and complex issues has received praise. Kohn applauded the fact that the show "toys with an incredibly sad subtext".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-indiewire_170-1"><a href="#cite_note-indiewire-170"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>166<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Novelist <a href="/wiki/Lev_Grossman" title="Lev Grossman">Lev Grossman</a>, in an interview with <a href="/wiki/NPR" title="NPR">NPR</a>, praised the backstory of the Ice King and the exploration of his condition in the third-season episode "<a href="/wiki/Holly_Jolly_Secrets" title="Holly Jolly Secrets">Holly Jolly Secrets</a>", the fourth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/I_Remember_You_(Adventure_Time)" title="I Remember You (Adventure Time)">I Remember You</a>", and the fifth-season episode "<a href="/wiki/Simon_%26_Marcy" title="Simon &amp; Marcy">Simon &amp; Marcy</a>", noting that his origin is "psychologically plausible".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-npr_173-0"><a href="#cite_note-npr-173"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>169<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Grossman praised the way the series was able to tackle the issues of <a class="mw-redirect" href="/wiki/Mental_illness" title="Mental illness">mental illness</a>, saying: "It's very affecting. My dad has been going through having <a href="/wiki/Alzheimer%27s_disease" title="Alzheimer's disease">Alzheimer's</a>, and he's forgotten so much about who he used to be. And I look at him and think this cartoon is about my father dying".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-npr_173-1"><a href="#cite_note-npr-173"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>169<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Critics have suggested that the show has grown and matured as it has aged. In a review of season four, for instance, Mike LeChevallier of <i><a href="/wiki/Slant_Magazine" title="Slant Magazine">Slant</a></i> magazine complimented the show for "growing up" with its characters.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-season4slate_174-0"><a href="#cite_note-season4slate-174"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He concluded that the series has "strikingly few faults" and awarded the fourth season three-and-a-half stars out of four.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-season4slate_174-1"><a href="#cite_note-season4slate-174"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The series has been included on a number of best-of lists. <i>Entertainment Weekly</i> awarded it second place in its 2012 list of "10 Best Cartoon Network Shows"<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-175"><a href="#cite_note-175"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>171<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and ranked it number 20 (out of 25) in a list of the "Greatest Animated TV Series".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-ewrev_167-1"><a href="#cite_note-ewrev-167"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>163<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-TVShowsOnDVD_176-0"><a href="#cite_note-TVShowsOnDVD-176"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>172<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Similarly, <i>The A.V. Club</i>, in a non-ranked run-down of the "best animated series ever", called the series "one of the most distinctive cartoons currently on the air".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-177"><a href="#cite_note-177"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>173<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The show has also received limited criticism from reviewers. LeChevallier, in an otherwise largely positive review of the third season for <i>Slant</i> magazine, wrote that "the short-form format leaves some emotional substance to be desired", and that this was inevitable for a series with such short episodes.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-season3slate_178-0"><a href="#cite_note-season3slate-178"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>174<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The independent cartoon scholar and critic David Perlmutter, who otherwise applauded the show's voice acting and its ability to surpass its source material, argued that the show's vacillation between high and low comedy epitomizes the fact that Cartoon Network is "unsure of what direction to pursue". He noted that "while some of [<i>Adventure Time</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s] episodes work well, others [are] simply confusing".<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-toons_13-3"><a href="#cite_note-toons-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 346">: 346 </span></sup> The newspaper <i><a href="/wiki/Metro_(British_newspaper)" title="Metro (British newspaper)">Metro</a></i> cited the show's frightening situations, occasional adult themes, and use of <a href="/wiki/Innuendo" title="Innuendo">innuendo</a> as reasons why parents might not want their young children watching it.<sup class="reference" id="cite_ref-179"><a href="#cite_note-179"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>175<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Industry_impact">Industry impact</h3></div>
